brain_regeneration.title: Transience implies ballisticity for uniformly elliptic i.i.d. RWRE (open, d >= 2) is a statement about the first moment of the regeneration time, and the polynomial condition (P)_M is a moment self-improvement
brain_regeneration.body:
PRIVATE REDUCTION, author-recorded. Under (IID)+(UE) transience in direction l gives the Sznitman-Zerner regeneration structure with tau_1 < infinity a.s.; ballisticity is E[tau_1 | D = infinity] < infinity (Drewitz-Ramirez Open Question 2.20). Under (UE) a trap of diameter r holds the walk at most exponentially long in r, so sub-ballistic behaviour needs polynomially rare traps of logarithmic size along the path, which i.i.d. environments do allow; the question is whether the tail P(tau_1 > n) can be as heavy as n^{-1+eps}. Open Question 3.20 (does positive velocity imply (P)_M for M > 15d + 5) is then the question whether a finite first moment of tau_1 self-improves to moments of order about M/d, because (P)_M is equivalent through the slab decomposition to high moments of tau_1. The Guerra-Ramirez theorem (T) <=> (T') (2018) settles Open Question 3.28 but neither of these. Recorded as the moment-self-improvement reformulation.
Random walk in i.i.d. uniformly elliptic environment on Z^d, d >= 2
Regeneration structure of Sznitman-Zerner

brain_regeneration.title: Attempt on Absolutely continuous invariant measure for the environment seen from the particle versus ballisticity
brain_regeneration.body:
ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Check both implications through the ergodic theorem for the environment process. Result: One direction is standard: if an invariant absolutely continuous probability measure Q exists and is ergodic, the ergodic theorem for the environment chain gives X_n/n -> E_Q[local drift] a.s., and transience in direction l plus Kozlov's theorem (Q equivalent to P, unique) makes the limit velocity well defined; it is nonzero in direction l provided E_Q[d(0,omega) . l] > 0, which follows from transience in direction l ONLY IF one also knows the velocity cannot vanish under transience, which is itself the ballisticity question, so this direction reduces to: invariant a.c. measure + transient in l implies v . l > 0. Under (E) the Kalikow-type argument gives v . l >= 0 but not strict positivity. The converse (ballistic implies invariant a.c. measure) is known under (UE) and (IID) from the renewal structure with finite expected regeneration time; under (ERG) only, regenerations are unavailable and the construction of Q fails. Both directions therefore reduce to statements known under (IID)+(UE) and unproved under (ERG)+(E). Obstruction: Without i.i.d. renewal structure neither the construction of the invariant measure nor strict positivity of the velocity is available.

brain_regeneration.title: Attempt on Ballisticity under the ellipticity moment condition
brain_regeneration.body:
ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine whether the moment condition controls the back-and-forth trap time and hence the regeneration-time tail. Result: The quantity 1/(1 - omega(0,e) omega(0,-e)) is the expected number of returns of the two-site back-and-forth excursion between 0 and e, so the moment condition bounds the expected holding time in two-site traps but not in larger traps (a trap of k sites in a line has holding time controlled by products of k such ratios, whose expectation is not bounded by the first-moment condition). Proposition 2.21 of the source shows the condition is necessary; sufficiency would need a bound on the expected time spent in traps of every size, i.e. on E[tau_1 | D = infinity]. A natural sufficient strengthening is a moment condition on the exit time from every finite box, which is implied by the two-site condition only under an additional assumption on the transition probabilities to move away. I therefore see the question as open in the sense that the two-site condition is strictly weaker than what the regeneration argument needs, and the Dirichlet case works because of the specific reversal identity of Dirichlet environments (Sabot's exit-time integrability). No new result. Obstruction: Two-site moment condition does not control larger traps; the Dirichlet argument uses a special reversal identity.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0042-ballisticity-under-the-ellipticity-moment-condition
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved

brain_regeneration.title: Attempt on Does positive velocity imply the polynomial ballisticity condition (P)_M?
brain_regeneration.body:
ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Relate (P)_M to the tail of the regeneration time. Result: (P)_M asks for a polynomial decay P(exit from a slab of width L against the direction l) <= L^{-M}; ballisticity is E[tau_1 | D = infinity] < infinity. A polynomial decay of the atypical exit probability with exponent M forces tail bounds P(tau_1 > n) <= n^{-M/(something)} through the standard slab decomposition, so (P)_M implies moments of tau_1 of order roughly M/d; conversely finite first moment of tau_1 gives, through the same decomposition, only the exit probability from a slab of width L bounded by L^{-1} type estimates, i.e. (P)_1, far below 15d + 5. So the question is equivalent to whether the first moment of the regeneration time automatically upgrades to moments of high order under (UE)+(IID), a self-improving property. Self-improvement is plausible because a heavy tail of tau_1 would require a trap structure incompatible with a positive velocity, but it is exactly the content of the open question and I have no proof. Recorded reduction: (P)_M for large M <=> E[tau_1^{M'}] < infinity for some M' growing with M, so the question is a moment self-improvement question. Obstruction: No self-improvement mechanism for regeneration-time moments is known.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0045-does-positive-velocity-imply-the-polynomial-ballisticity-condition-p-m
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved

brain_regeneration.title: Attempt on Zero velocity on the non-transient event for excited random walks
brain_regeneration.body:
ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Try to derive it from the law of large numbers structure of Theorem 4.8. Result: Theorem 4.8 gives lim X_n/n in {v, -cv} a.s. under a 0-1 law assumption for the directional events; on the non-transient event the walk returns to a bounded region infinitely often, so liminf |X_n|/n = 0 trivially along the return times, and the question is whether limsup X_n . l / n can be positive: the walk would have to make excursions of linear size and return. For Markovian RWRE the analogous statement (Zerner 2002) uses a regeneration argument; for excited walks the excursions of linear size would, on the non-transient event, be repeated infinitely often through the same (partially eaten) environment, and each long excursion in direction l has probability decaying exponentially in its length by a large deviation bound for the walk in a fixed (already modified) environment, IF the environment modification is bounded (bounded stacks) - so under (BD) the expected number of linear excursions from a bounded region is finite by Borel-Cantelli, giving the answer YES under (BD) plus a uniform large-deviation bound for excursions. Without (BD) (unbounded stacks under (EL) only) the modification of the environment can be unbounded and the large deviation bound is not uniform. Recorded: under (IID), (EL) and (BD) the answer is yes provided the uniform excursion large-deviation estimate holds (plausible from the elliptic Markov comparison since eaten cookies only change transition probabilities within [eps, 1-eps]); the general (EL) case without (BD) is the open part. Key identity: Linear excursions from a bounded region have exponentially small probability uniformly under (BD)+(UEL); Borel-Cantelli gives zero velocity on the recurrent event. Obstruction: Uniformity fails without bounded stacks.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0133-zero-velocity-on-the-non-transient-event-for-excited-random-walks
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved

brain_Sznitman.title: Attempt on Transience of i.i.d. elliptic RWRE in dimensions d >= 3
brain_Sznitman.body:
ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Try to derive transience from the quenched invariance principle route used for balanced walks, in the general case. Result: For balanced environments Lawler's argument uses the invariant measure of the environment process (from the maximum principle) to get a quenched CLT and then transience via the Green function decay; for general elliptic i.i.d. environments no invariant measure absolutely continuous with respect to P is known to exist (its existence is Open question 2.19's territory), so the route fails at the first step. An alternative is the Lyapunov-exponent route: transience follows if the quenched Green function G_omega(0,0) is finite a.s., which for a random walk with bounded-range transitions in d >= 3 follows from a lower bound on the spectral gap of the walk killed outside large boxes; in a random environment the killed walk's Perron eigenvalue could be arbitrarily close to 1 if the environment contains near-recurrent regions, and under (E) alone such regions exist at all scales with small probability. A quantitative bound needs the density of such traps to decay fast enough with their size, which is a large-deviation statement about the i.i.d. environment that I could not verify without (UE). Under (UE) the trap analysis of Bolthausen-Sznitman-Zeitouni suggests transience should hold but no proof exists. No result. Obstruction: No invariant measure for the environment process; trap density under mere ellipticity uncontrolled.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0043-transience-of-i-i-d-elliptic-rwre-in-dimensions-d-3

Directional transience implies ballisticity
OpenAI
September 23, 2026
Abstract
We prove that almost-sure transience in a fixed direction implies a deterministic
limiting velocity with positive projection in that direction for nearest-neighbor random
walks in independent and identically distributed uniformly elliptic environments on Zd,
d ≥2. This resolves the ballisticity conjecture positively.

1.2
Context and significance
Theorem 1.1 resolves positively the ballisticity conjecture for iid uniformly elliptic nearest-
neighbor environments in dimension at least two. Fribergh and Kious [8, Conjecture 1.1]
formulate it with precisely the one-direction transience assumption used here. The distinction
between escape and speed is essential: already in one dimension, uniformly elliptic iid
environments can give a transient walk with zero speed; see Solomon [19] and the discussion
in [21, p. 510]. The higher-dimensional conjecture asks whether the additional spatial routes
prevent this form of slowdown.
The regeneration construction of Sznitman and Zerner [22] separates the walk at new
height records below which it never returns. After an initial piece, the resulting pieces are
independent with a common conditioned law; see also [21, Section 1] and [8, Section 2]. A
finite mean duration then gives a velocity by the renewal law of large numbers. Almost-sure
finiteness of the pieces does not supply that mean. The proof here first controls a piece’s
spatial radius—its greatest distance from its starting point— and only later its duration.
Zeitouni’s survey [23] gives further background on this distinction and the regeneration
method.
Several quantitative routes to ballisticity precede the present result. Kalikow’s auxiliary-
walk approach [12] led to sufficient directional drift conditions. Under Kalikow’s condition,
Sznitman [20] obtained slowdown estimates and a central limit theorem through regeneration-
time tails. His conditions (T)γ and (T ′) require stretched-exponential control of backward
slab exits in nearby directions, and his effective criterion gives a finite-box characterization of
(T ′) yielding positive speed [21]. Berger, Drewitz, and Ramírez [3] proved that sufficiently
strong polynomial exit bounds imply (T ′). Guerra and Ramírez [11] proved (T ′) ⇒(T),
where (T) is the exponential slab-exit condition. Guerra’s later preprint [10, Definition 1.4
and Theorem 1.9] gives a finite-box criterion already implied by backward-exit probabilities
of order o(L1−d) in nearby directions. These results start from quantitative exit assumptions.
Theorem 1.1 starts with almost-sure escape in one direction and derives the quantitative
crossing estimate needed for finite mean duration.
Even the spatial intermediate conclusion requires care. Simenhaus [18, Theorem 1] obtains
a deterministic asymptotic direction from transience in a nonempty open set of directions.
Our spatial-radius estimate uses the specified single direction and gives a limiting ray before
a duration moment has been proved. The record-counting proof is related to the cone-renewal
argument in [18, Lemma 2]; its treatment of arbitrary real projected heights is given directly
in Section 2.
The two-walk construction has a close precedent in the common spatial regeneration levels
of Rassoul-Agha and Seppäläinen [16, Section 7]. Comparing shared and independent copies

1.3
Proof strategy
The proof separates spatial control from control of elapsed time. Section 2 constructs true
record words in the original real direction. Counting ordinary record indices gives finite mean
projected width, even when projected heights are not discrete. A forward template at a
tilted record then gives finite mean spatial radius. This produces a deterministic limiting ray
without a duration moment and permits a signed coordinate permutation so that height is x1.

aN < N−β decays faster than every power of N. The same section proves that this estimate
supplies the missing duration moment and hence Theorem 1.1. The rest of the paper proves
the estimate.
Sections 3 and 4 compare two walks at first hits of integer layers. Independent common
regeneration words give symmetric increments and a scale defined by their truncated variance.
On Gaussian subsequences, a shared-environment comparison must exclude positive limiting
occupation on the projected diagonal. Its cutoff-scale argument also controls the smaller scales
that need not be Gaussian. The resulting two-copy limit yields a quenched approximation
without assuming a second moment or a pre-existing quenched invariance principle.
Section 5 combines Gaussian and non-Gaussian subscales to retain positive quenched
mass whose first-hit positions lie in narrow tubes at every large scale. Section 6 turns this
into separated endpoint seeds, rapid-loss bounds, and an outward-order estimate with an
exponentially integrable local remainder. All adaptive tests use only departure rows below
their tested top layer.
If (5) fails, conditioning on its bad environments costs only logarithmic relative entropy.
The multiscale stages of Section 7 then give a positive expected loss of global survival mass
on episodes with bounded stage count. Each episode is an adaptively chosen stretch of layers;
the bound on its stage count also controls the logarithm of its height. In Section 8, averaging
over episodes gives a stationary law of local endpoint profiles and their upper environments.
Entropy bounds exclude diffuse mass and infinitely many separated profile classes on the
positive-drop event. A tail-order statistic in a surviving full-support class contradicts the
sustained drop: testing far out in its two tails removes the local environmental bias from the
outward-order remainder. This contradiction proves (5) and completes the speed argument.

2.2
Finite spatial radius and the limiting ray
The finite mean width controls progress only at true boundaries. To control the path between
them, we prove that the spatial radius of a word also has finite mean. The argument compares
two bounds for a large displacement relative to the running height maximum. An infinite
mean radius would make such a displacement occur with probability of order 1/B. At each
new ratio threshold, however, there is a fixed positive chance of a fresh continuation that caps
the ratio until the walk leaves the height strip. Iterating these chances gives an exponentially
small upper bound in B.
